concept.name: Secrets Management & Vaults

relationships.description: Connects Secrets Management & Vaults to api security oauth2 in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: A centralized secrets manager like HashiCorp Vault encrypts static credentials behind a Shamir-unsealed barrier and issues short-lived, dynamically generated credentials (e.g., 1-hour PostgreSQL roles or 15-minute STS tokens) via workload identity (Kubernetes JWT/IAM) with automatic lease revocation.
spark.keyTakeaway: Replace static, long-lived .env passwords with identity-bound dynamic leases (15m-1h TTL) and Transit encryption-as-a-service so leaked credentials expire before attackers can pivot.

concept.whyItMatters: Hardcoded API keys in Git repositories, Kubernetes Secrets (which are merely base64-encoded in etcd unless KMS-encrypted), and shared static DB passwords turn a single container compromise into permanent lateral movement. Vault centralizes audit logging, automates rotation without app restarts, and shrinks credential blast radius from years to minutes.
whenToUse: Production workloads requiring dynamic, per-pod database credentials, cloud IAM STS tokens, or short-lived mTLS X.509 certificates.
Regulated environments (PCI-DSS, SOC 2, HIPAA) demanding immutable audit logs of every secret read and cryptographic key rotation.
Multi-cloud or hybrid Kubernetes fleets needing a unified identity broker (SPIFFE/OIDC/K8s SA) rather than vendor-locked secret stores.
whenNotToUse: Public, non-sensitive configuration flags (feature toggles, log levels, public endpoints)—use ConfigMaps or a config service.
Tiny single-developer prototypes where running an HA Raft Vault cluster with auto-unseal adds unnecessary operational overhead over cloud-native KMS/Secrets Manager.
Client-side browser or mobile apps—secrets shipped to untrusted user devices are always extractable; use OAuth2 PKCE and backend proxies.
keyPoints: Vault's storage backend (Raft/Consul) holds only AES-256-GCM ciphertext; the root key resides in RAM behind a seal barrier unlocked via Auto-Unseal (AWS/GCP KMS) or Shamir's Secret Sharing.
Dynamic Secrets (Database/AWS engines) generate ephemeral credentials on demand (e.g., CREATE ROLE v_app_9f2a WITH VALID UNTIL ...), eliminating shared static passwords.
Workloads authenticate via platform identity—Kubernetes ServiceAccount JWTs, AWS IAM signed requests, or AppRole—never a static root token.
Vault Agent Sidecar or CSI Driver renders secrets into in-memory tmpfs (/vault/secrets) and renews leases at ~2/3 TTL without writing to disk.
The Transit Secrets Engine acts as encryption-as-a-service, keeping PII encryption keys inside Vault so applications never hold raw DEKs/KEKs.

examples.title: Eliminating Static Postgres Passwords in Kubernetes
examples.scenario: A fintech platform with 80 microservices shared 4 static PostgreSQL passwords across ConfigMaps; rotating a password required coordinated restarts and caused 15-minute outages.
examples.outcome: Deploying Vault's PostgreSQL dynamic secrets engine with Vault Agent sidecars issued unique 1-hour DB roles per pod, renewed transparently in tmpfs, cutting rotation downtime to zero.

examples.title: Zero-Trust PII Encryption with Vault Transit
examples.scenario: Compliance auditors flagged that 12 services held raw AES encryption keys in environment variables for encrypting customer national IDs.
examples.outcome: Migrating to Vault's /v1/transit/encrypt endpoint kept keys inside Vault's HSM-backed barrier with automated key versioning and full per-call audit trails.

tradeOffs.factor: Dynamic Ephemeral Secrets vs Cached Static Secrets
tradeOffs.pro: Each pod gets unique credentials with automatic 15m-1h expiration and instant per-lease revocation.
tradeOffs.con: Requires Vault and the target DB's admin connection to be reachable when pods scale up or renew leases.

tradeOffs.factor: Sidecar/CSI tmpfs Injection vs Direct SDK Calls
tradeOffs.pro: Apps stay Vault-agnostic by reading standard files from memory-backed tmpfs (/vault/secrets).
tradeOffs.con: Apps must still reload files on SIGHUP/inotify when leases rotate, or risk using expired credentials.

tradeOffs.factor: Self-Hosted HA Vault vs Cloud-Native Secrets Manager
tradeOffs.pro: Vault supports dynamic DB roles, PKI, SSH, and Transit across AWS, GCP, and on-prem from one control plane.
tradeOffs.con: Requires operating a 3-5 node Raft cluster, KMS auto-unseal, snapshot backups, and HA upgrades.

failureModes.name: Vault Sealed or Unreachable During Pod Scale-Out
failureModes.description: If Vault seals after a node reboot without Auto-Unseal, or loses quorum, new pods fail authentication and cannot fetch DB credentials.
failureModes.mitigation: Run a 3-5 node Integrated Storage (Raft) cluster across 3 AZs with Cloud KMS Auto-Unseal and enable Vault Agent persistent caching for graceful grace-period reads.

failureModes.name: Lease Explosion Exhausting Database Roles
failureModes.description: High-churn batch jobs or crash-looping pods request thousands of dynamic DB roles with 24h TTLs, hitting PostgreSQL's max_roles or connection limits.
failureModes.mitigation: Keep dynamic role TTLs short (15m-1h), revoke leases explicitly on pod SIGTERM, and enforce max_ttl caps on the Vault database role.

failureModes.name: Secret Leakage via Swap, Env Vars, or Crash Dumps
failureModes.description: Injecting secrets into process environment variables exposes them in /proc/<pid>/environ, core dumps, and accidental log dumps.
failureModes.mitigation: Mount secrets strictly via memory-backed tmpfs (CSI/Sidecar), enable MLOCK on Vault nodes to prevent swap writes, and scrub logs.

failureModes.name: Over-Privileged Vault Policies (Wildcard Paths)
failureModes.description: Granting secret/data/* to a CI runner or microservice lets any compromised pod read production keys for unrelated teams.
failureModes.mitigation: Scope HCL policies strictly to secret/data/prod/<service>/* bound to specific Kubernetes namespace + ServiceAccount claims.

commonMistakes: Storing Vault root tokens or unseal keys in CI/CD variables or alongside backups.
Passing secrets as container environment variables instead of tmpfs files or in-memory API responses.
Neglecting to configure Vault audit devices (file/syslog), which causes Vault to block requests if a sole audit sink fills disk.
Using Vault purely as a static KV store without enabling dynamic leases or automated rotation.
Forgetting to reload database connection pools when Vault Agent rotates a dynamic credential file on disk.

sections.content:
## The idea

Centralized secrets management separates **who** a workload is from **what** credentials it holds. Instead of baking static passwords into images or `.env` files, a secrets manager like **HashiCorp Vault** verifies a workload's cryptographic platform identity (a Kubernetes ServiceAccount JWT or AWS IAM signature) and issues a scoped, short-lived token.

Everything inside Vault sits behind an AES-256-GCM **seal barrier**: storage backends only ever see ciphertext, while the master encryption key lives strictly in memory (`mlock`ed to prevent swap leakage) and is unlocked via Cloud KMS Auto-Unseal or Shamir's Secret Sharing.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider a Kubernetes pod `orders-api` needing PostgreSQL access via **Vault Agent**:

1. **Workload Auth**: On pod start, Vault Agent reads the projected ServiceAccount JWT (`/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token`) and posts it to Vault's `auth/kubernetes/login` endpoint.
2. **Identity Verification**: Vault validates the JWT against the Kubernetes `TokenReview` API, confirms namespace=`prod` and SA=`orders-sa`, and returns a Vault token bound to policy `orders-db-read` with a `1h` TTL.
3. **Dynamic Credential Generation**: Vault Agent requests `database/creds/orders-role`. Vault connects to PostgreSQL over mTLS and executes `CREATE ROLE "v-k8s-orders-a8f1" WITH LOGIN PASSWORD '...' VALID UNTIL '...'`.
4. **Tmpfs Rendering & Renewal**: Vault Agent writes the ephemeral username/password to `/vault/secrets/db.conf` on an in-memory `tmpfs` volume and renews the lease at `2/3` TTL (`40m`).
5. **Revocation**: When the pod scales down, the lease expires (or is explicitly revoked), and Vault drops the PostgreSQL role automatically.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Static KV vs Dynamic Secrets vs Transit
sections.content:
## Static KV vs Dynamic Secrets vs Transit

Not every secret can be generated dynamically (e.g., third-party Stripe or Twilio API keys). Structure your secrets architecture across three tiers:

- **KV v2 (Versioned Static)**: For external API keys, with automated rotation webhooks or dual-key grace periods.
- **Dynamic Engines**: For databases, AWS STS, RabbitMQ, and internal PKI X.509 certificates—zero shared secrets, automatic expiry.
- **Transit Engine**: For encrypting application data (PII, SSNs) via API (`/v1/transit/encrypt`) using envelope encryption, so application servers never hold raw AES keys in memory.

## Secret delivery patterns compared

| Pattern | Blast Radius | Disk / Env Exposure | Rotation Mechanics | Operational Overhead |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Static Env Vars / K8s Secrets** | Months-Years | High (`/proc`, etcd) | Manual pod restarts | Minimal |
| **CSI Driver / Sidecar (`tmpfs`)** | Minutes-Hours | None (RAM only) | Auto-renewed; app reloads file | Moderate (sidecar/DaemonSet) |
| **Dynamic Ephemeral Leases** | 15m-1h per pod | None (RAM only) | Per-lease expiry + auto-DROP ROLE | High (requires Vault + DB admin role) |
| **Transit Encryption-as-a-Service** | Zero key exposure | None (keys stay in Vault) | In-place key version rotation | Moderate (RPC per encrypt/decrypt or DEK wrap) |

## Failure modes

- **Audit Log Backpressure Outage**: Vault guarantees that no authenticated request succeeds if all configured audit devices fail to write. If a single file-based audit sink fills `/var/log`, the entire Vault cluster halts—always configure dual audit sinks (e.g., syslog/fluentd + file with logrotate).
- **Connection Pool Credential Drift**: When Vault Agent rotates `/vault/secrets/db.conf`, an app that only reads config at startup will fail auth once the old lease expires. Use `SIGHUP` reloaders or pool `before_connect` credential hooks.
- **Stale Shamir Unseal**: Relying on manual 3-of-5 human keyholders to unseal nodes during an overnight AZ outage turns a 2-minute node replacement into a 45-minute incident—use Cloud KMS Auto-Unseal.

## High availability and disaster recovery

Deploy Vault as a 3- or 5-node **Integrated Storage (Raft)** cluster across 3 availability zones:

- Only the Raft leader handles writes; standby nodes forward writes or serve read-only performance standby traffic.
- Schedule automated encrypted Raft snapshots (`vault operator raft snapshot save`) to S3/GCS every `15m` and test restores quarterly.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Enable Cloud KMS Auto-Unseal and disable/revoke the initial root token after bootstrap.
- [ ] Authenticate workloads via Kubernetes SA JWT, OIDC, or AWS IAM—never static tokens.
- [ ] Use dynamic secret engines (15m-1h TTL) for databases and internal PKI wherever supported.
- [ ] Mount secrets into RAM-backed `tmpfs` via Vault Agent or CSI driver; avoid container environment variables.
- [ ] Configure at least two independent audit devices so one full disk cannot halt Vault.
- [ ] Enforce least-privilege HCL policies scoped to exact service namespaces and paths.

interviewProblems.title: Secrets Management & Vaults
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Secrets Management & Vaults. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: A centralized secrets manager like HashiCorp Vault encrypts static credentials behind a Shamir-unsealed barrier and issues short-lived, dynamically generated credentials (e.g., 1-hour PostgreSQL roles or 15-minute STS tokens) via workload identity (Kubernetes JWT/IAM) with automatic lease revocation.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Vault HA Cluster applies the primary invariant and coordinates with PostgreSQL Primary.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, PostgreSQL Primary experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Run a 3-5 node Integrated Storage (Raft) cluster across 3 AZs with Cloud KMS Auto-Unseal and enable Vault Agent persistent caching for graceful grace-period reads.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Replace static, long-lived .env passwords with identity-bound dynamic leases (15m-1h TTL) and Transit encryption-as-a-service so leaked credentials expire before attackers can pivot.
Avoid trap: Storing Vault root tokens or unseal keys in CI/CD variables or alongside backups.
Avoid trap: Passing secrets as container environment variables instead of tmpfs files or in-memory API responses.
When to reach for it: Production workloads requiring dynamic, per-pod database credentials, cloud IAM STS tokens, or short-lived mTLS X.509 certificates.
When to reach for it: Regulated environments (PCI-DSS, SOC 2, HIPAA) demanding immutable audit logs of every secret read and cryptographic key rotation.

putItTogether.title: Putting Secrets Management Vault Together
putItTogether.summary: Replace static, long-lived .env passwords with identity-bound dynamic leases (15m-1h TTL) and Transit encryption-as-a-service so leaked credentials expire before attackers can pivot.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Secrets Management Vault before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Deploying Vault's PostgreSQL dynamic secrets engine with Vault Agent sidecars issued unique 1-hour DB roles per pod, renewed transparently in tmpfs, cutting rotation downtime to zero.
